question: AC-3 finishes on a problem and every domain still has at least one value. What can you conclude?
options: A solution exists: take any value from each domain
No solution exists unless every domain is a single value
Nothing definite yet: arc consistency is necessary but not sufficient, so search is still needed
The problem has exactly one solution
explain: A non-empty arc-consistent network may still have no solution, as the triangle of pairwise inequalities over two values shows. An empty domain proves infeasibility, but a full one proves nothing. Search, with propagation at each node, settles the question.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: What ships in an image: base images, distroless and scanning
question: A distroless image has no shell. What is the most important security effect of that?
options: It prevents the kernel from running system calls
It encrypts the filesystem
It makes the image impossible to exploit
After exploiting the app, an attacker has no ready interpreter or tools inside the container to continue with
explain: The app can still have bugs, but the classic next step (open a shell, download tools) has nothing to work with. It raises the attacker's cost; it does not remove the need to patch the app.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: A hardened pod spec, line by line
question: A pod sets `runAsNonRoot: true` and nothing else in its security context. Its image contains a setuid-root helper. Which missing setting would block the helper from raising privileges?
options: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, which sets no_new_privs
automountServiceAccountToken: false
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
hostUsers: true
explain: no_new_privs makes the kernel ignore the setuid bit on exec. allowPrivilegeEscalation defaults to true, so it must be set explicitly to false.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
question: A cluster on AWS uses IRSA for every app, but pods can still reach the instance metadata service. What can an attacker in any pod do?
options: Fetch the node's IAM role credentials from IMDS and act with the node role's permissions
Read other clusters' Secrets
Nothing; IRSA disables IMDS
Only read their own role's credentials
explain: AWS's docs say containers have access to the node IAM role when IMDS is not restricted. IRSA adds a better path; it does not close the old one. Block or limit IMDS for pods too.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Exposed dashboards, kubelets and Docker APIs
question: Tesla's attackers kept CPU usage low and used an unlisted pool behind a CDN on a non-standard port. Which detection was hardest for them to evade?
options: A port-based firewall rule for well-known mining ports
An alert when CPU exceeds 90%
A process-level rule that flags known miner binaries or mining protocol command lines, combined with egress allowlists
A blocklist of known mining pool domains
explain: Each listed evasion targets one simple signal: domain lists, IP reputation, port rules, CPU alarms. Watching what processes run and allowing only expected outbound connections does not depend on those surface features.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: A container is a process with a narrowed view
question: Which statement about a container and a virtual machine running on the same node is correct?
options: Both run their own kernel, so a kernel panic affects only one of them
The container has its own scheduler, so cgroup limits are advisory
The container's threads are scheduled by the host kernel, which also serves their page faults and TCP connections
A container cannot share a CPU with other work
explain: The container's threads are plain tasks on the host kernel's run queues. That is what makes containers start in milliseconds, and also what makes the node's kernel shared fate for everything on it. A virtual machine does run a second kernel, at the cost of booting one.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Probes, Services and DNS: liveness is not readiness
question: Every replica of a service uses one endpoint for both liveness and readiness, and that endpoint returns HTTP 503 (Service Unavailable) while the database is unreachable. The database restarts for 90 seconds. What happens?
options: Only readiness is affected, so traffic pauses and then resumes
The Service keeps routing, because liveness does not touch EndpointSlices
The scheduler moves the pods to other nodes
Every replica fails liveness and is restarted together, so recovery is delayed by cold starts on top of the database outage
explain: A liveness failure restarts the container; a readiness failure only removes it from the EndpointSlices. Because one shared endpoint drives both, a dependency outage triggers both everywhere at once: the fleet goes NotReady and is also restarted, so every replica returns cold. Liveness should test only the process; readiness is the right place to admit a dependency is down.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
question: Shown list v4 is [J4, J12, J5]. The user says *hide the Hooli one*, and the assistant shows [J4, J12]. The user then says *open the second one*. Which job should open?
options: J5, because it was second in the original search
J12, because it is second in the list currently on screen
J12, because the tracker remembers it from the previous turn
Ask a clarifying question every time
explain: Ordinals refer to the most recent list the user saw, here shown v6 = [J4, J12]. J12 happens to be second in both lists, but the reason it is right is the current list; the third option names the right job for the wrong reason, and would fail if the lists differed.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Hidden computation: filler tokens, encoded reasoning, paraphrasing
question: In the toy scheme, a paraphraser keeps each opening word with probability 0.8 and otherwise picks either synonym at random. About how many of the 8 hidden bits can still be sent reliably?
options: 8 bits, because most words survive
6.4 bits, since 80% of words are kept
About 4.25 bits
0 bits, since any rewrite destroys the code
explain: Each bit flips with probability e = (1 - 0.8)/2 = 0.1, because a rewritten word is still right half the time. Capacity is 1 - H2(0.1) = 0.531 bits per sentence, so 8 x 0.531 = 4.25 bits. 6.4 ignores that the decoder does not know which bits flipped; 0 bits needs k = 0.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Building and scoring a CoT monitor
question: You want a 1% false-positive rate for a new monitor. Where should the threshold come from?
options: The 99th percentile of scores on known attack transcripts
A fixed score of 50, the middle of the 0 to 100 scale
The 99th percentile of the monitor's scores on clean runs from the same agent and tasks
The score that maximizes AUROC
explain: FPR is measured on clean runs, so the threshold is their 99th percentile, as Arnav et al. did. Attack scores set recall, not FPR. A fixed 50 means different FPRs for different monitors and agents. AUROC is threshold-free, so no threshold maximizes it.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Pinned host memory: the precondition for overlap
question: Which of these is a sound pinning policy for a server that handles 64 concurrent requests?
options: Call cudaHostRegister on every request buffer as it arrives and unregister on completion
Pin two staging buffers per worker stream, sized to one chunk, and reuse them for every request
Pin the whole request arena at startup so no request ever needs staging
Skip pinning and rely on the driver's staging buffer, which is pinned anyway
explain: A small set of long-lived, reused staging buffers gets the asynchrony with bounded pinned footprint. Per-request registration pays the pinning cost on the critical path for every request; pinning a whole arena takes RAM away from the OS, which both NVIDIA and PyTorch warn against; and relying on the driver's staging buffer keeps the copy synchronous, which is exactly what we are trying to avoid.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: A worked pipeline: four chunks, and the copy-bound crossover
question: You chunk the host decode too, and measure the host stage at 8.00 ms per chunk (kernel stays 6.00 ms). What paces the pipeline and what is the 4-chunk time?
options: The host, at 8.00 ms per chunk: 18.25 + 3 x 8.00 = 42.25 ms
The kernel, at 6.00 ms per chunk: 18.25 + 3 x 6.00 = 36.25 ms
Neither; the host runs on a different device so it does not enter the makespan
The H2D copy, since it is the stage directly after the host
explain: The host is just another single-server stage in the pipeline, and the makespan is set by whichever stage is largest. At 8.00 ms it overtakes the 6.00 ms kernel, giving (8.00 + 4.00 + 6.00 + 0.25) + 3 x 8.00 = 42.25 ms, with 2.00 ms of SM idle per chunk. The fix is more host parallelism (more decode threads or loader workers), not more CUDA streams.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Host memory as a tier: unified memory, zero-copy and offloading
question: A 2 GB embedding table fits in GPU memory and every step reads thousands of rows from it. Someone proposes mapped pinned memory to save the startup copy. What happens?
options: It gets faster, because no copy engine is involved
Nothing changes; mapped memory is cached on the GPU after the first access
It runs at the same speed as long as the host buffer is pinned
Every step pays link latency and bandwidth for every row read, again and again; copy it to GPU memory once instead
explain: Mapped pinned memory is not cached on the GPU, so reused data crosses the link on every access, at higher latency and lower bandwidth than GPU memory. The guide says mapped memory should not be considered a performant alternative for the majority of a kernel's memory needs. One copy at startup is paid once and every later read is local.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
question: You switch from a BERT-based reranker to an XLM-RoBERTa-based one and keep the same max_length. Which detail changes in packing?
options: The query is now placed after the document
There are no special tokens at all
The model accepts 1,024 positions automatically
The pair uses four special tokens and no segment ids, so one fewer document token fits
explain: XLM-RoBERTa packs a pair as <s> A </s></s> B </s> and does not use token type ids. Order and the max_length you pass stay the same; the budget for the document shrinks by one token.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
question: A colleague proposes caching cross-encoder scores for every (query, document) pair to remove reranking latency. When does this actually help?
options: Only for repeated exact queries (head queries) over an unchanged candidate set; the long tail of new queries still pays full cost
Always, because cross-encoder scores never change
Never, because the scores depend on batch size
Only if the model uses sigmoid outputs
explain: A score is a function of the exact query and document text. Caching works for frequent repeated queries, which Hofstatter et al. also note as the exception, but most queries in real traffic are unique and must be scored live.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key
question: Why does a one-time pad not replace AES for HTTPS (encrypted web traffic)?
options: Because XOR is too slow on modern CPUs
Because the key must be as long as all the traffic and delivered securely in advance
Because it was broken by quantum computers
Because it cannot encrypt binary data
explain: The pad is unbreakable but its key logistics are impossible at internet scale. Practical ciphers use a short key (16 or 32 bytes) and accept security based on computational difficulty.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Hash functions: fingerprints, avalanche and the birthday bound
question: Roughly how many random inputs until a collision is likely for a 160-bit hash such as SHA-1, if the hash were ideal?
explain: Birthday bound: about 2^(n/2) = 2^80. Real attacks on SHA-1 do better than that by exploiting its structure.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
question: Which Python call should generate a password-reset token?
options: random.getrandbits(128)
secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
uuid.uuid1()
hash(time.time())
explain: secrets reads the OS CSPRNG. random is predictable from its state or seed, uuid1 encodes time and the machine address, and hashing the time adds no entropy.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto
question: A teammate proposes encrypting session cookies with AES-CTR and a counter stored in memory that resets to 0 on restart. Which rule does this break?
options: Do not hash passwords
Never reuse a nonce: after a restart the same counter values repeat under the same key, and CTR also lacks authentication
Use constant-time comparison
Retire SHA-1
explain: A counter that resets repeats keystreams (two-time pad), and plain CTR gives no integrity, so cookies could be bit-flipped. Use an AEAD with random or persistent nonces, or a vetted token library.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Bleichenbacher and ROBOT: retiring RSA key exchange
question: A legacy appliance only supports TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA and the vendor will not patch it. Which action addresses the risk best?
options: Add a random delay to its TLS error handling
Switch the appliance to a 4096-bit RSA key
Enable more cipher suites so clients avoid RSA
Move the service behind a TLS terminator that offers only ECDHE with AEAD suites, using a key the appliance never holds
explain: Random delays average out, and a longer key does not change the padding oracle. Terminating TLS in front of the appliance with modern suites, and a key the appliance does not share, removes the vulnerable code path. ROBOT noted some appliances could not be used securely at all.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Secret-dependent timing: comparisons, Minerva and TPM-Fail
question: Why did a leak of only the bit-length of k, a few bits per signature, lead to full key recovery in Minerva?
options: Because lattice techniques combine small leaks from hundreds or thousands of signatures into the full key
Because the bit-length reveals the private key directly
Because the smart card also reused k
Because the leak let the attacker read memory
explain: Each signature known to have a short k carries a little information about the private key; lattice methods combine many such signatures to solve for it. The paper reports 500 to 2,100 signatures, depending on the noise.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Reviewing crypto code: safe APIs, tests and migration
question: A review finds `Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.CTR(nonce))` with `nonce = os.urandom(16)` and no MAC, used to encrypt session data stored in a cookie. Which change addresses the most important problem?
options: Use a 32-byte nonce
Replace it with an AEAD such as AESGCM or Fernet so modified cookies are rejected
Switch CTR to CBC
Base64-encode the ciphertext
explain: The random 16-byte CTR nonce is acceptable for uniqueness; the missing integrity is the real flaw, since the client holds the cookie and can modify it. CBC is also unauthenticated, and encoding changes nothing.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
question: A TiledMMA uses the SM80 16x8x16 FP32-accumulate atom with a 2x2 layout of atoms (4 warps) and no value repetition. How many FP32 accumulators does each thread hold?
explain: Each atom is one warp computing 16x8 = 128 accumulators over 32 threads, so 4 per thread. A 2x2 layout of atoms adds more warps, not more values per thread: 128 threads cover 32x16 = 512 accumulators, still 4 each.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load
question: A vendor ships a card with a CXL controller and 256 GB of DRAM and no compute engine. Which protocols must it implement?
options: CXL.cache only
CXL.io and CXL.mem
CXL.io and CXL.cache
CXL.mem only, because CXL.io is optional
explain: This is a Type 3 memory expander. It needs CXL.io for discovery and configuration (every device does) and CXL.mem so the host can load and store its memory. It has no cache of host memory, so CXL.cache is not needed.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
question: Pond allocates a VM's predicted untouched memory from the pool and exposes it as a zero-core NUMA node. Why the zero-core node rather than mixing pool and local memory in one node?
options: Because CXL memory cannot be part of a node that has CPUs
Because the guest OS then prefers its local node and touches the pool only when it needs more, so correctly predicted untouched memory costs nothing
Because hypervisors cannot map CXL memory into guest page tables
Because it makes the pool memory persistent
explain: With a uniform address space the guest would scatter allocations across pool and local memory. A CPU-less node is a fallback in Linux's default policy, so the guest fills local memory first; if the untouched-memory prediction is right, the pool slices are never touched.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: View source is not hacking: the Missouri teachers' SSNs (2021)
question: A reporter views page source on a public US state website and finds exposed personal data. Which risk does the Missouri case show remains even after Van Buren?
options: None: Van Buren makes all viewing of public pages legal everywhere
Only copyright claims
Only a civil CFAA suit
A broader state computer crime statute and public accusations, even if no gate was broken
explain: Van Buren interprets one federal statute. State laws such as Missouri's 569.095 use different words, including 'intentionally examines information about another person'. The prosecutor declined, but the case shows the risk is real.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Copyright and trade secrets: DMCA section 1201 and Megamos Crypto
question: In Volkswagen v Garcia, what mainly concerned the court, as CyBOK describes it?
options: That the researchers had sliced the chip
That the algorithm was weak
That the algorithm was recovered from third-party software that may have existed through trade secret misappropriation
That the paper was written in English
explain: CyBOK notes the court seemed to accept that recovering the algorithm from the chip itself would raise no case. The problem was the provenance of the software the researchers used.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Professional ethics: ISC2, ACM, the Menlo Report and the UMN patches
question: Which Menlo principle most directly captures the kernel maintainers' main objection to the UMN experiment?
options: Justice
Respect for law and public interest
Respect for persons
Beneficence
explain: Respect for persons is operationalised through informed consent. The maintainers were unwitting subjects of an experiment on their review behaviour.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Excess loss: measuring how much a domain can still be learned
question: Why does DoReMi use a reference model of the same size and architecture as the proxy, rather than a tiny bigram model as DRO-LM did?
options: So the two losses are on a similar scale and their difference is meaningful
Because bigram models cannot compute log-likelihood
To make the reference model share weights with the proxy
explain: The paper says it uses a same-size reference so the losses are on a similar scale. A much weaker reference would leave large excess loss everywhere and blur the signal.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Knobs, failure modes, and what came after DoReMi
question: Two teams run DoReMi on the same corpus, one with a 50k-vocabulary tokenizer and one with a 256k vocabulary, and get noticeably different weights. Is something broken?
options: Yes, DoReMi should be tokenizer-independent
Yes, one of them forgot to average over steps
No, weights are token proportions and per-token losses, both of which change with the tokenizer
explain: Domain weights are defined by token counts and excess loss is per token. Different tokenizers split domains into different numbers of tokens, so the weights legitimately differ. The DoReMi repo calls this out explicitly.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
question: After exact and near deduplication, your forum domain shrinks from 20B to 8B unique tokens. You keep its learned weight of 0.04 in a 1T-token run. What changed?
options: Its epochs went from 2 to 5, past the roughly 4 where repetition is nearly free, so recompute the weights or cap the domain
Nothing, because the weight is unchanged
Its epochs halved, because duplicates no longer count
The domain is now read less than once
explain: 0.04 x 1T = 40B tokens. Before dedup that was 40 / 20 = 2 epochs; now it is 40 / 8 = 5 epochs. Dedup removes copies from the data, but a fixed weight brings the repetition straight back through extra epochs.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes
question: You double the track to 256 keys but keep the same layouts. How large is the SoA times array, in 64-byte lines?
options: 8 lines
32 lines
64 lines
16 lines
explain: 256 time values at 4 bytes each = 1,024 bytes = 16 lines. The AoS array would be 256 x 16 = 4,096 bytes = 64 lines, still 4 times larger, because each record is 4 times the size of a time.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Finding sensitive data: inventories, patterns, checksums and context
question: Why is the Luhn check useful in a discovery tool even though it offers no security?
options: It can only be computed by the card issuer
It encrypts the number
It cheaply discards about 90% of random digit strings before more expensive context checks
It identifies the card's owner
explain: Luhn was designed to catch transcription errors. Any 15 digits have exactly one valid check digit, so random strings pass only about 10% of the time: a cheap filter that cuts noise before the detector looks for keywords and dates.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Searching encrypted data: deterministic encryption and enclaves
question: What does attestation give a client of a secure enclave?
options: Encryption of data in transit
Evidence, checked before any keys are shared, that the enclave is genuine and runs the expected code
A backup of the column master key
A guarantee that no side channel exists
explain: Attestation is how the client decides the enclave is genuine and runs the expected code. It is not transport encryption or key backup, and it does not prove the hardware is free of side-channel weaknesses.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Where DLP acts: endpoints, email, web and cloud
question: A company wants to stop customer data being uploaded to personal cloud drives. Its web proxy does not decrypt TLS. Where can it still enforce this?
options: Nowhere: TLS makes uploads invisible
At the destination cloud provider's servers
In the email gateway
In the endpoint DLP agent and managed browser, which see the file before it is encrypted for upload
explain: Without TLS interception the proxy cannot see content, but the endpoint agent sees the file and the upload attempt on the device itself, before TLS. That is the 'upload to restricted cloud service domain' activity in Microsoft's endpoint DLP.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a data security programme, and practice
question: A company encrypts every database with TDE, runs DLP on email, and has never run discovery. Which lesson-1 gap remains widest?
options: Data in transit
The databases' backups
Side-effect copies (exports, tickets, shares, buckets) that nobody knows exist, so no control is applied to them
Outbound email
explain: TDE protects the known databases and their backups against stolen media, and email DLP covers one channel. Without discovery, copies elsewhere are unprotected and unmonitored: the Pegasus pattern.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: What Internet honeypots see: noise, bots and reused passwords
question: Two thirds of the passwords bots tried were already in a breach corpus. Which defence does this support most directly?
options: Rejecting passwords that appear in known breach lists
Forcing password changes every 30 days
Hiding the SSH banner
Moving SSH to a different port
explain: Bots mostly replay leaked and default passwords. Blocking breached passwords removes them; forced periodic changes and port moves do little against list-based guessing.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Deception in Active Directory: honey accounts and honey SPNs
question: Why is "any 4769 event where ServiceName is the decoy" a far better rule than "many 4769 events with RC4"?
options: RC4 tickets are never requested legitimately
Event 4769 is only logged for decoys
No legitimate client ever requests the fake SPN, so the decoy rule has almost no benign matches, while RC4 requests have legitimate sources such as old systems
The decoy rule also blocks the request
explain: Metcalf notes some systems and trusts still use RC4, so the volume rule needs tuning. The decoy turns "potential" into "definite" because only an enumerating intruder asks for it. It detects; it does not block.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Measuring value: the Tularosa study, metrics and practice
question: Your decoy dashboard shows zero alerts in a year. Which follow-up question matters most?
options: Should we remove the decoys to save money?
Did we test each decoy end to end in that year, and did the test alerts reach a person?
Can we make the decoys produce more alerts?
Are the decoys on the Internet?
explain: Silence is only good news if the decoys demonstrably work. Untested decoys may have been broken for months.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Seeds and RNG state: a different problem from kernels
question: Two requests arrive with the same seed and the same temperature, and the sampler draws from one shared RNG stream. What does request B's token depend on?
options: How many draws the sampler already consumed for other requests, so B's token depends on the traffic around it.
Nothing beyond its own seed, since the seed fully determines the stream.
Only the temperature, because the seed is consumed once at startup.
The order in which atomic adds landed in the final GEMM.
explain: A shared stream makes the position in the stream part of the request's input, and that position is set by the queue. Seeding the stream fixes the sequence of numbers, not which element of it your request receives. Per-request generator state is what removes the dependency.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce
question: Jepsen-style fault injection and DST both inject partitions and crashes into real code. What does DST add that changes day-to-day debugging most?
options: It tests a formal model instead of the code, so it is exhaustive
Any failing run can be replayed exactly from its seed
It needs no changes to how the system does I/O
It runs on real hardware, so timing is realistic
explain: Determinism is the key addition: a failure becomes a seed you can replay, step through and add logging to. DST does test the real code (not a model), it usually *does* require routing I/O through simulated interfaces, and its timing is simulated, not real.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
question: Which system is the *weakest* fit for designing DST in from the start?
options: A new replicated log written in-house with its own network and disk layer
A large existing service built on many third-party clients, thread pools and direct system calls
A consensus library whose I/O already goes through small traits
A storage engine with a single-threaded event loop
explain: Designing DST in requires every source of nondeterminism to be pluggable, which is hard to retrofit across many dependencies and threads. The Antithesis docs call it generally impractical for systems already in production; that is the case a deterministic hypervisor targets. The other three are close to the FoundationDB and TigerBeetle shape.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Least-privilege pipeline credentials: tokens, environments, secrets
question: A deploy key is stored as a JSON document with three fields in one secret. A tool prints the parsed `private_key` field on error. What happens in the log?
options: It is probably shown: redaction matches the exact stored string, and one field of the parsed JSON is a different string
It is masked, because the whole secret is masked
The job fails before printing
GitHub deletes the log automatically
explain: GitHub warns that structured data makes redaction fail because redaction largely relies on finding an exact match. Store each sensitive value as its own secret.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Reviewing infrastructure as code: reading a Terraform plan
question: A reviewer reads only the HCL diff in a PR, which changes a variable default from `10.0.0.0/16` to a module input. Why should the pipeline also check the plan JSON?
options: The plan JSON holds the resolved values, such as the CIDR the module actually produces, while the HCL only shows a reference
The HCL diff is always longer
Plan JSON is required by Git
HCL cannot contain security groups
explain: Values from variables, modules and data sources are only known after planning. Scanning the plan catches what the source hides behind references.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Sentinel, enforcement levels and guardrails developers accept
question: A new rule would block 40 pull requests a week across the company, and nobody has seen its results yet. Which enforcement level should it start at?
options: Hard mandatory, so the problem is fixed fastest
Advisory, to measure impact and fix false positives before anything blocks
Soft mandatory with no override permission
No policy at all
explain: Advisory is Sentinel's default and lets a policy fail with a warning. Starting there turns the unknown 40 a week into a measured list before teams are blocked.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?
question: What does the 'absorbing state' in masked diffusion refer to?
options: The final layer of the Transformer that absorbs all positional information
The [MASK] token: once the forward process masks a token, it stays masked
The end-of-sequence token that stops generation
A Gaussian noise vector added to token embeddings
explain: In D3PM's absorbing-state process every token moves to [MASK] at some point and never leaves it. At the final time the sequence is entirely masked, which gives a simple known starting point for generation.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
question: You set Fast-dLLM's threshold so that, in a hard reasoning span, no masked token reaches it. What does the sampler do?
options: It commits the single most confident token, so it degrades gracefully to one token per pass
It stalls until the model becomes more confident
It commits every token in the block anyway
It restarts the block with a new random seed
explain: The threshold rule always unmasks the highest-confidence token to guarantee progress. In uncertain regions the sampler becomes sequential, which is exactly where dependencies between tokens matter most.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
question: Your summarization service has a 15 s TTFT SLO and a 0.15 s TPOT SLO. Attainment is failing. Which change most likely helps?
options: Protect decode steps from long prefills (separate decode GPUs or smaller prefill chunks)
Give prefill more tensor parallelism to cut TTFT
Lower the TTFT SLO to 5 s
Batch more prompts into each prefill
explain: With a 15 s TTFT budget, prefill is rarely the binding constraint. The long documents create long prefills that stall decode steps and break the TPOT SLO, which DistServe observed for vLLM on LongBench, a benchmark of long-document tasks. Shielding decode is the fix; batching more prompts would make the stalls worse.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Disaggregation at scale: MoE, expert parallelism and elastic pools
question: After a product launch, prompts get 4x longer while output lengths stay the same. In a disaggregated deployment with a load-based autoscaler, which pool should grow, and which signal moves first?
options: Decode, first seen as rising TPOT
Neither: the P:D ratio depends only on the request rate
Prefill, first seen as queued prefill tokens and rising TTFT; decode KV utilization climbs later as the larger caches arrive
Both equally, first seen as GPU utilization
explain: Prefill work per request grows at least 4x (more with attention), so the prefill share of GPU time rises, as in the 08 to 14 window of the timeline. Requests queue at prefill before anything reaches decode, so queued prefill tokens and TTFT move first, the signal Dynamo's load-based planner watches. Each request also brings 4x more KV, so decode KV-cache utilization rises next and decode may need capacity too.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: What deleting a file really does: a FAT walk-through
question: After deletion, which piece of the PHOTO.JPG directory entry is gone for good?
options: The first character of its name
Its size
Its first cluster number
Its extension
explain: Deletion overwrote only the name's first byte with 0xE5. Size, first cluster and extension remain, which is why tools show deleted names as ?HOTO.JPG or _HOTO.JPG.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Linux ext4: superblock, inodes, extents and the journal
question: With the default data=ordered journal mode, what can the ext4 journal give you after a file is deleted?
options: Possibly an older copy of the metadata block holding the file's inode, with its extents
A full copy of the file's content
Nothing, because the journal is erased on deletion
The user name of whoever deleted it
explain: data=ordered sends metadata, not file data, through the journal. Older inode blocks in the journal can point recovery tools to the content blocks. ext4 does not log who deleted a file.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Shortcuts, Jump Lists, ShellBags and the Recycle Bin
question: The USB stick is lost. What can still show that the user browsed its folder `E:\Q3`?
options: Only the stick itself
The master file table of the laptop's C: drive
SRUM
ShellBags in the user's hives, and LNK and Jump List entries pointing to `E:\Q3`
explain: ShellBags record navigated folders, and LNK and Jump List entries record opened files with their paths and volume serial, all stored on the laptop. The laptop's C: MFT does not index files on E:.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics from the defender's side: what each trick leaves
question: Why does wiping a file often fail to hide that something was wiped?
options: Wiping tools are blocked by NTFS
The wipe overwrites the content but leaves traces such as the tool's execution artefacts and change journal records of the overwrite
Wiped data can always be recovered by carving
Windows keeps a copy of every wiped file in SRUM
explain: SP 800-86 notes wiping is effective at preventing collection of the content itself, so carving does not undo it. But running a tool and rewriting a file leave execution and journal traces. SRUM stores usage statistics, not files.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
question: A DiskANN service is limited by SSD IOPS at peak traffic, and p99 latency is comfortably under target. Which change is most sensible?
options: Increase W from 4 to 16
Increase L to raise recall
Lower W toward 1 to cut total reads per query
Turn off re-ranking
explain: Smaller beams waste fewer reads, so each query consumes less of the IOPS budget; latency rises but there is headroom. The repository docs recommend W = 1 for the highest throughput at a fixed IOPS rating. Re-ranking costs no extra reads, so disabling it saves nothing.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
question: In the toy example, what happens to the optimal policy as $\beta$ grows very large?
options: It approaches the reference distribution: 50%, 30%, 20%
It puts all mass on B, the highest reward
It becomes uniform over A, B and C
It puts all mass on A, the reference's favorite
explain: Reweighting by $\exp(r/\beta)$ approaches multiplying everything by 1 as $\beta$ grows, so the optimum returns to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. At $\beta = 10$ it is already 49.38%, 32.75%, 17.87%. Small $\beta$ is what collapses it onto B.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
question: Your feedback log has 2,000 thumbs-up and 20,000 thumbs-down responses. Following the KTO paper's guidance with $\lambda_U = 1$, which $\lambda_D$ is in range?
options: 0.1, to down-weight the rare class
1, the default
explain: The ratio $\lambda_D n_D / (\lambda_U n_U)$ should land in [1, 1.5]. With $n_D/n_U = 0.1$, $\lambda_D$ must be between 10 and 15, so 12 fits. Leaving it at 1 lets the undesirable class dominate the gradient.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
question: Dual writes have been on for a week, but the backfill has not run. A read from the new Subscriptions table for a customer who subscribed two years ago and has not changed since returns nothing. What happened?
options: The dual write to the new table failed for this customer
Nothing went wrong: untouched old objects only reach the new store through the backfill
The new table needs a read replica before it can serve reads
Dual writes copy old rows lazily on the first read, so the next read will succeed
explain: Dual writes only cover writes made after they were turned on. Stripe also copied objects lazily whenever they were *updated*, but an object nobody touches is copied only by the backfill. This is why reads must not move until the backfill and a completeness check are done.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
question: Midway through phase 3, the new write path for prorations is found to compute the wrong amount. Most other paths already write the new store first and archive to the old one. What is the safest response?
options: Restore the new store from last night's backup
Pause all writes until the bug is fixed
Delete the old store so the two cannot disagree
Flip the prorations path back to the old write order; the old store is still current because every path still writes it
explain: In phase 3 every write still reaches the old store (as the primary or as an archive), so it is complete. Rolling one path back by a flag is cheap. That safety disappears in phase 4, which is why it comes last.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: X3DH's fine print: signed prekeys, replay, deniability, misbinding
question: An initial message that used no one-time prekey is replayed to Bob. What must the post-X3DH protocol do?
options: Nothing; AEAD stops replays
Randomize Bob's encryption key with fresh input from Bob before Bob sends
Ask the server to delete the message
Switch to RSA
explain: A replay makes Bob derive the same SK again. If Bob encrypted under it directly, two sessions would share keys. The spec says the follow-on protocol MUST randomize Bob's key, which the Double Ratchet does with a fresh DH ratchet key.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Post-quantum ratcheting: Signal's SPQR and iMessage PQ3
question: Why does PQXDH alone not protect a conversation against a recorded-traffic quantum attacker who also stole the device's state once?
options: PQXDH uses a weak KEM
PQXDH only covers group chats
Healing after the theft comes from X25519 DH ratchet steps, which the quantum attacker can recompute from recorded public keys
The server stores the root key
explain: With the state, the attacker knows the root key; recorded ratchet public keys plus discrete logs give every later DH output. Only fresh post-quantum secrets during the conversation (SPQR, PQ3's rekeying) break that chain.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Group chats: pairwise fan-out, sender keys, and who decides membership
question: What does a stolen sender key let an attacker do?
options: Read all past group messages
Read every member's messages forever
Nothing, sender keys are signed
Read that member's future group messages until the sender key is replaced, typically at the next membership change
explain: The hash ratchet gives forward secrecy, so past keys are safe. But without a DH ratchet there is no healing; the chain continues until the group resets sender keys, which WhatsApp does when a member leaves.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Backups and cloud copies: the quiet way around E2EE
question: Bob's iMessage threads are E2EE, and Bob uses standard iCloud Backup with Messages in iCloud. Who can recover Bob's message history from Apple's servers?
options: Nobody, iMessage is end-to-end encrypted
Only Bob's contacts
Apple, because the backup includes the Messages in iCloud key and Apple holds the backup keys under standard protection
Only someone with Bob's unlocked phone
explain: Apple's own overview says the backup includes that key and that standard-protection backup keys are held in Apple data centers. Advanced Data Protection changes this by making the backup itself end-to-end encrypted.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Lawful access and client-side scanning
question: A proposal says scanning happens "on the device, so encryption is not weakened". What is the strongest technical objection?
options: The plaintext is analysed and results leave the device, so whoever controls the matcher or its database gains a surveillance channel, and the matcher can be fooled
Phones are too slow
Scanning breaks the Double Ratchet
Perceptual hashes are post-quantum
explain: The cipher is untouched, but the end is no longer private. Bugs in our Pockets argues CSS neither guarantees crime prevention nor prevents surveillance, and NeuralHash research showed collisions can be forced or avoided.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: The verifier: proving every path safe before it runs
question: A program loops `for i in 0..N` where N is read from a map value with no upper bound check. The verifier rejects it. Why?
options: Maps cannot be read inside loops
Loops are never allowed in eBPF
The verifier cannot prove the loop terminates within its limits, because N could be any 64-bit value
The JIT does not support loop instructions
explain: Bounded loops are allowed (since v5.3) only if the verifier can show the exit condition is reached within its 1M processed-instruction budget. An unbounded N defeats that proof. Clamping N to a small constant first fixes it.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: The three budgets a model must fit on a small device
question: A model has 250,000 int8 weights (244 KB) and its largest operator reads a 40 KB tensor and writes a 40 KB tensor. The target has 256 KB of flash and 64 KB of SRAM. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, both fit
The weights do not fit in flash
The peak activations (80 KB) do not fit in SRAM
The model must be fp32 to run on a CPU
explain: Weights live in flash: 244 KB is under 256 KB, though tight once code is added. Activations need the peak of input plus output, 80 KB, which is more than 64 KB of SRAM. You would shrink the largest feature map (fewer channels or lower resolution), not the weights.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
question: You replace every 3x3 conv in a model with depthwise separable blocks and the MAC count drops 8x, but measured latency on your phone CPU drops only 2x. Which explanation is most plausible?
options: The MAC formula is wrong
Depthwise layers do few MACs per byte moved, so they are limited by memory traffic and kernel efficiency rather than arithmetic
Separable convolutions use more parameters
Latency always scales exactly with MACs, so the measurement must be wrong
explain: MAC counts ignore memory traffic and kernel quality. A depthwise layer does only k x k MACs per input value, so it is often bound by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic. This is why the pipeline ends with measurement on the device.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Pulse Secure and FortiOS, 2019: file reads that leaked passwords
question: An organisation patched its Pulse appliance in May 2019 and saw no alerts afterwards. In 2020 an attacker logs in through it as a real employee. What was missing?
options: A second firmware upgrade
Resetting every password that could have been read from the appliance before the patch, and requiring MFA
A reboot after patching
A stronger TLS cipher
explain: The patch stopped new file reads. Passwords already copied stayed valid until changed, and without MFA a password alone was enough to log in. This is exactly CISA's AA20-107A finding.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Exposure management: what you show the internet, continuously
question: Why combine an outside-in scan with the asset inventory instead of trusting either one alone?
options: The scan finds what is really exposed, including unknown devices; the inventory supplies owners and true versions. Each corrects the other
Scans are always more accurate than inventories
Inventories are required by law, scans are not
It makes the scan faster
explain: Equifax's scans missed a vulnerable system (prerequisite course), and inventories miss devices people set up without telling anyone. The join of the two is what produces actionable, owned findings.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Responding to a compromised appliance: evidence, rebuild, rotate
question: After a confirmed PAN-OS compromise, which item is most often forgotten in rotation?
options: The firewall's local admin password
The firewall's directory service account, which in Volexity's case was a domain admin
The firewall's hostname
The firewall's public IP address
explain: Admins remember the local admin password, but service accounts configured on appliances are easy to overlook because no person logs in with them. Volexity saw exactly such an account used to reach the domain controllers. Hostnames and addresses are not secrets.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Why RL makes reasoning long: the length bias in the policy loss
question: PPO with gamma = 1, lambda = 0.95 and value estimates near 0 sees a failed response (reward -0.5). Its per-token-averaged loss is about 0.099 at 100 tokens. About what is it at 1,000 tokens, and which way does that pull length?
options: About 0.010: the loss falls like 1/T, so longer failed responses are favored
About 0.99: the loss grows with T, so shorter responses are favored
About 0.099: GAE makes the loss independent of length
About -0.010: the sign flips once the response is long enough
explain: The leading term is $-R/(T(1-\lambda)) = 0.5/(T \times 0.05)$: 0.1 at T = 100 and 0.01 at T = 1,000 (exactly 0.0994 and 0.0100 in the code). A smaller loss for a longer failure is the pull toward length.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
question: A request needs 4,800 reasoning tokens and a 400-token answer at its effort level. With max_output_tokens = 3,000 it fails; you retry at the same effort with the cap raised to 6,000. How many output tokens are billed in total for the two calls?
explain: The failed call bills its 3,000 reasoning tokens and returns no answer. The retry generates 4,800 + 400 = 5,200, all billed as output. Total 8,200. Lowering effort, not tightening the cap, is how you pay for fewer thinking tokens.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: HTML character references and the order a browser decodes
question: A filter rejects attributes whose text contains `javascript:`. Which attribute text gets past it but still produces a `javascript` scheme in the browser?
options: `https://a.example/javascript:`
`JAVASCRIPT:go()` after the filter lower-cases
`javascript:go()`
`javascript%3Ago()`
explain: The HTML parser turns `j` into `j` before the URL parser runs. The https URL only has `javascript:` in its path (and the filter blocks it anyway). A lower-casing filter catches `JAVASCRIPT:`. In `javascript%3Ago()`, `%3A` is not decoded when the scheme is parsed, so there is no `javascript:` scheme.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Lossy conversion: Windows Best-Fit and PHP CVE-2024-4577
question: In the toy, why does the check `arg.startswith("-")` miss the attack?
options: Python's `startswith` ignores invisible characters
The child process strips the first character
The soft hyphen is a dash in every encoding
The check runs on the wide string, and only the later ANSI conversion turns U+00AD into `-`
explain: At check time the first character is U+00AD, which is not `-`. Best-Fit mapping happens afterwards, on the way to the ANSI command line, so the check and the child see different strings.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: URL parser differentials: one URL, two hosts
question: Your redirect check uses Python's `urlsplit` and an exact host match; the browser follows the URL. Which input class is still most likely to cause a disagreement?
options: A plain `https://good.example/path`
URLs with a query string
URLs containing backslashes or control characters, which the URL Standard handles differently from many libraries
Upper-case scheme names like `HTTPS`
explain: Backslashes and control characters are exactly where WHATWG repair rules and other libraries diverge. Ordinary paths, queries and scheme case are handled the same by both.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Defender's checklist for encodings and parsers, and where to practise
question: A team fixes a reported bypass by adding the attacker's exact input to a blocklist. Why is that a weak response?
options: Blocklists are slow
Blocklists cannot hold Unicode
The underlying differential remains, so other spellings of the same meaning will still pass
It is a strong response if the list is reviewed monthly
explain: The bug is the disagreement between a check and a later reader. As long as it exists, an attacker can find another encoding, normalisation or parser quirk that produces the same effect.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: ETW: providers, sessions and consumers
question: A server's PowerShell Operational log has had no 4104 events for two days, while the same server shows normal process activity in Sysmon. What is the best first reading?
options: A possible logging gap or tampering worth checking, because silence from one source while others continue is itself a signal
Nothing happened: no one used PowerShell
Sysmon must be broken instead
4104 events are only written on domain controllers
explain: No PowerShell use for two days may be true, but a source going quiet while others continue is exactly how disabled providers or changed policies look. Check the logging policy and the provider state before concluding nothing happened.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: WMI: remote execution, event subscriptions and their telemetry
question: Sysmon logs events 19, 20 and 21 within a minute on a finance laptop, naming a CommandLineEventConsumer. What is this most likely to be?
options: Normal Windows Update activity
A user printing a document
Sysmon restarting after a crash
A permanent WMI event subscription being created: filter, consumer and binding, a known persistence technique (T1546.003)
explain: Events 19, 20 and 21 are filter, consumer and binding registration. Together, with a command-line consumer, they describe a full permanent subscription. Legitimate ones are rare on workstations, so investigate who created it.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Credential hardening: LAPS, LSA protection and Credential Guard
question: An intruder dumps the local Administrator hash on one LAPS-managed laptop. What does LAPS change about their next step?
options: Nothing, LAPS only protects domain accounts
LAPS deletes the local Administrator account
LAPS encrypts LSASS memory
The hash works only on that laptop, because every machine's local admin password is different, and it changes again on rotation
explain: LAPS gives each device a unique, rotated local admin password, so a hash from one machine does not authenticate to the others. It does not protect LSASS itself; that is LSA protection's and Credential Guard's job.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: XDR, MDR and running EDR well: the HSE lesson
question: At HSE, antivirus detected Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz on 31 March but nothing was blocked. According to the review, why?
options: The antivirus did not recognise either tool
The workstation was offline
Cobalt Strike disabled the antivirus first
It was set to monitor mode, so it recorded but did not block
explain: The PwC review, as summarised by Krebs, says the antivirus detected both tools but was set to monitor mode, so it did not block the malicious commands. Detection without blocking or response left the attacker six more weeks.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Scoring a disaggregation: MAE, NEP, NDE and F1
question: Two models have the same fridge MAE. Model A is off by 5 W on every sample; model B is exactly right except for a few samples off by a lot. Which metric separates them, and how?
options: NDE: B scores worse because squaring weights its few large errors more
F1: A scores lower because small offsets flip the on/off labels
NEP: A scores worse because it has more errors
None: equal MAE means every normalised metric is equal
explain: NEP is MAE times T divided by total energy, so equal MAE means equal NEP. NDE squares errors, so B's few large misses count more. F1 barely moves for A, since a 5 W offset on a 120 W fridge does not cross the 10 W on/off threshold.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Blocking: compare only pairs that could match
question: Adding a third rule, *same city*, to our toy blocking would do what?
options: Raise pairs completeness to 1.0 and keep the candidate count at 10
Recover r6-r7 (both Denver) but add many more pairs, lowering the reduction ratio
Have no effect, because city is not a name field
explain: City is low-cardinality (it has few distinct values): everyone in Austin would be paired with everyone else in Austin. It recovers r6-r7 but at a large cost in comparisons on real data. A stricter combined key (city plus name prefix of 2 letters, say) is the usual compromise.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
question: A tenant has 3 Global Administrators, all eligible through PIM, but 14 users hold Application Administrator permanently, and one app they manage has the Graph permission RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory. What is the real number of paths to Global Administrator power?
options: 3: only the Global Administrators
0: PIM eligibility blocks all paths
14: but only if those users also hold Helpdesk Administrator
At least 17: any Application Administrator can add a credential to that app and use its permission to assign roles
explain: Microsoft's role reference warns that Application Administrators can add credentials to an app and act as it. An app with RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory can assign roles, so each of the 14 is a path, plus the 3 eligible admins.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
question: A thief steals a refresh token issued to a mail client that Ana consented to for Mail.Read and Files.Read. What can the thief obtain?
options: Only mail access tokens, because the token was issued for Exchange
Nothing without Ana's MFA
Only an ID token
Access tokens for any resource the client was granted for Ana, including files
explain: Microsoft documents refresh tokens as bound to user and client, not to a resource. The client can redeem it for access tokens to any resource where it holds permission, and the MFA claim from Ana's original sign-in carries over.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
question: A tenant's only Conditional Access policy requires MFA for 'All users' and excludes the group 'Service Accounts'. An attacker sprays passwords. Which account is the most valuable target?
options: A regular user, because MFA is optional for them
The emergency access account, because it has no MFA
A guest user
An account in 'Service Accounts': a correct password is enough, because no policy applies to it
explain: Excluded accounts are evaluated by no policy, so a sprayed password suffices. Emergency accounts should be protected by a phishing-resistant credential, not by Conditional Access; service accounts need managed identities or workload policies instead.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A hardening baseline, an incident runbook, and where to practise
question: During an incident you find a malicious multitenant app with Mail.Read (application) in your tenant. What is the right first action on the app?
options: Delete the app's service principal
Reset the passwords of all users
Ask the app's publisher to delete the application object
Disable the service principal so it cannot obtain tokens or be consented to again, then remove its grants and investigate what it read
explain: Microsoft's consent playbook says to disable rather than delete: a deleted service principal can return when someone consents again, while a disabled one cannot get tokens. Then remove its grants and scope its access in the logs.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
question: An ET server reads one 4096-byte chunk per event and then returns to epoll_wait. A client uploads 10,000 bytes in one burst and waits for a reply. What happens?
options: The server reads all 10,000 bytes over three wakeups
epoll_wait returns EAGAIN
The kernel splits the burst into three separate edge events
The server reads 4096 bytes and may never be woken for the remaining 5904, so the client hangs
explain: Once all the bytes are queued, nothing new arrives after the first 4096 are read, so there is no new edge, and epoll_wait can block forever with 5904 bytes in the buffer. This is exactly step 5 of the epoll(7) example. Fix: read until EAGAIN, or until a short read on a stream socket.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set
question: Your team trains a learned reranker on click logs from January to June and evaluates on 300 labeled queries sampled from the same months. Which leak is most likely to inflate the test score?
options: The test queries use graded rather than binary labels
Many test queries, or close paraphrases of them, also appear in the training clicks
The test set is too large for a bootstrap confidence interval
The reranker uses a cross-encoder instead of a bi-encoder
explain: Popular queries repeat. A reranker trained on clicks for a query has effectively seen its answer. Split by query cluster and preferably by time (train on earlier months, test on later), so test queries are genuinely new. A 300-query set is not too large to bootstrap (lesson 4), and the reranker's design (a cross-encoder reads query and document together, a bi-encoder embeds each separately) does not create a leak.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Stack canaries: a tripwire in front of the return address
question: Why does the compiler insert the canary check just before `ret` rather than right after `strcpy`?
options: Because strcpy itself checks the canary
Because the return address is only used at ret, so checking just before it guards that use whatever code wrote to the frame
Because the check is free at ret but costly elsewhere
Because the canary is only written at the end of the function
explain: The canary protects the return address, and the return address is only consumed by ret. Checking just before ret covers every write that happened anywhere in the function body, not just one call. The cost is the same anywhere; strcpy knows nothing about canaries.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: RELRO, the GOT and FORTIFY_SOURCE
question: A binary is built with partial RELRO only. An attacker has a bug that writes 8 chosen bytes to a chosen address. Which table is still a useful target, and which flag closes it?
options: The stack canary; -fstack-protector-all
The PLT stubs; -Wl,-z,noexecstack
.got.plt, left writable for lazy binding; -Wl,-z,now (full RELRO)
.text; -fPIE
explain: Partial RELRO leaves .got.plt writable so lazy binding can fill it in. Adding -z now makes the loader resolve everything at start-up so the whole GOT can be made read-only.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Kernel mitigations: SMEP, SMAP, KASLR, KPTI and EternalBlue
question: According to Microsoft's analysis, which change made EternalBlue as leaked fail on the newest 64-bit Windows 10 even before patching?
options: The HAL region it relied on was no longer executable and its address was randomized
SMBv1 was removed from Windows 10
Windows 10 used stack canaries in the kernel
The NSA patched the exploit
explain: The exploit placed its payload in the HAL region at a known, executable address, which held on Windows 7. Windows 10 made that memory non-executable and the latest 64-bit builds randomized it. The SMBv1 bug itself remained until MS17-010 was applied.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
question: Two threads write different fields of one struct that fits in a single cache line. A colleague says this cannot be slow because nothing is shared. What is the best reply?
options: Right, the compiler places each field on its own line automatically
Right, only atomic variables can cause cache contention
Wrong, but only because the struct needs a mutex
Wrong, the fields share one cache line, so each write forces the line to move between cores
explain: Compilers pack fields together to save space; they do not spread them across lines. Any write needs the whole line, so the two cores fight over it. No mutex is needed for correctness here, because the fields are distinct; the problem is purely performance.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: How big is a line, how to find false sharing, who pads
question: Why might a library avoid the C++17 constant `hardware_destructive_interference_size` in a public header?
options: Its value can change with compiler tuning flags, so separately built code may disagree on struct layout
It is not defined in C++17
It is always 64, which is too small
It only works with std::atomic members
explain: GCC sets it from -mtune, and its documentation warns that all translation units relying on it must use the same tuning. In a public header that is an ABI hazard, so libraries often use a fixed constant such as 128 instead.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Cheaper rounds and smarter servers: compression and FedOpt
question: On the skewed split with E = 5, a colleague replaces FedAvg with a well-tuned FedAdam and expects the toy to reach 2.3. Where does it converge, if it converges?
options: To 2.3, because adaptive steps correct client drift
To about 1.944, the same fixed point, because the averaged delta is zero there whatever the server does
To 1.667, the average of the local optima
It cannot converge, since Adam needs true gradients
explain: At 1.944 the clients' moves cancel in the weighted average, so the pseudo-gradient is zero and every server optimizer stops there. Server optimizers change speed and stability. To move the destination you must change what clients compute: less local work, a proximal term, or SCAFFOLD's control variates (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Threats: what updates leak and how clients poison the model
question: An auditor argues that FedAvg's 5 local epochs per round make client updates safe to share in the clear. Based on the Inverting Gradients experiments, what is the best reply?
options: Correct: after 5 epochs the update no longer depends on individual examples
Correct only for convolutional networks
Wrong: 5 local epochs were no harder to invert than 1; only more images per update made reconstruction harder, and not safe
Wrong, because local epochs make updates larger and therefore easier to invert
explain: Geiping et al. found single-image reconstructions unimpeded even after 100 local steps, and their 8-image experiments were no harder at 5 epochs than at 1. Averaging over more images lowered quality, but some images from a batch of 100 were still recognizable. Formal protection needs differential privacy.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-gamma: expand every neighbor list by gamma
question: Why does ACORN-gamma skip HNSW's RNG-based pruning when building neighbor lists?
options: It makes construction too slow
The pruned detour through a third node may fail the predicate, so the shortcut it relied on vanishes in the predicate subgraph
RNG pruning only works for cosine distance
HNSW never prunes at the bottom level
explain: HNSW drops edge v to b if some kept neighbor a is closer to b, trusting search to go v, a, b. For a predicate where v and b pass but a fails, that path does not exist. Without knowing predicates at build time you cannot prune safely, so ACORN keeps the near neighbors and uses a predicate-agnostic compression instead.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Fine-grained experts: split each expert into m slices
question: A team trains a small MoE at a modest budget and finds that $G = 16$ trains slower in wall-clock time than $G = 8$, though $G = 16$ has slightly lower loss per step. Which reading fits the scaling-law paper?
options: Granularity never helps; the law is wrong
Per-step loss keeps improving with $G$, but routing and small-matrix overhead grow with $G$, so the wall-clock optimum can sit at a lower $G$, especially for small models
$G = 16$ must have more active parameters
The loss improvement comes from more total parameters
explain: Finer experts keep active and total parameters fixed, so the per-step gain is real but diminishing. Krajewski et al. saw exactly this: at 64 x 7M, $G = 8$ beat $G = 16$ in wall-clock time because routing cost dominated. Higher $G$ pays off at larger budgets.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Putting it together: routing in DeepSeek-V3
question: A team copies V3's recipe but trains with very small global batches (a few sequences per step). Which risk grows most?
options: Future-token leakage from the bias
The shared expert stops training
Node-limited routing stops working
Per-step load imbalance, since batch-wise balancing cannot even out a batch that is mostly one domain, so busy experts stall the step
explain: The loss-free paper shows balance improving as the computation batch grows, and the V3 report lists imbalance within small batches as a challenge that large-scale expert and data parallelism (model copies each training on a different slice of the batch) solves. The bias uses only past batches, so there is no leakage.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: SPI flash, SMM and the write lock LoJax walked through
question: Why was RwDrv.sys useful to the LoJax operators?
options: It is a validly signed driver that gives low-level hardware access, so Windows loads it
It exploited a Windows kernel bug
It disables Secure Boot
It encrypts the SPI flash
explain: The driver belongs to a legitimate utility and carries a valid signature, so the kernel loads it. Its job is to read and write hardware registers, which is exactly the access a flash writer needs.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: The 2023 to 2026 Microsoft certificate rollover
question: A kiosk PC never received the 2023 certificates. What happens after the 2011 certificates expire in 2026, according to Microsoft?
options: It stops booting immediately
Secure Boot switches itself off
It keeps booting, but can no longer receive new boot manager, db, dbx and boot-level security updates
The TPM is cleared
explain: Expiry does not stop the existing chain from booting. The device simply falls off the update path, so future boot-level fixes never reach it.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Hardware roots of trust: Boot Guard, AMD PSB and Apple silicon
question: LoJax wrote a modified firmware image into SPI flash. On a machine with Intel Boot Guard in verified mode with the OEM key fused, what would most likely happen at the next boot?
options: Secure Boot would catch the new DXE driver
The ACM would find the firmware's initial boot block no longer verifies against the OEM key, and the policy would stop the boot
Nothing, Boot Guard only measures
The TPM would erase the implant
explain: ESET states that with Boot Guard available and properly configured, the machine would have refused to boot after the compromise. Secure Boot, which runs inside the modified firmware, would not.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Firmware updates, resilience and the BMC beside the CPU
question: A firmware update tool verifies the vendor's signature but accepts any signed version. Which NIST SP 800-147 recommendation does it miss?
options: Secure local update
Rollback prevention: refusing authentic but older images with known weaknesses
Non-bypassability
None
explain: 800-147 says the authenticated update mechanism should prevent rollback to an earlier authentic version with a known security weakness, for example by comparing version numbers.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3: producer and consumer warps, then ping-pong
question: A teammate proposes giving the producer warpgroup as many registers as the consumers, "to be fair." What is the most likely effect?
options: Faster loads, because TMA needs registers for each byte copied
No effect, because register counts are fixed per kernel
Fewer registers for the consumers, forcing smaller tiles or spills in the math path
Better ping-pong, because both warpgroups can then do softmax
explain: TMA is issued by a single thread and copies data without staging it in registers. Registers given to the producer are taken from the consumers, which hold the accumulators; the paper deallocates producer registers and reallocates them to consumers for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 backward, determinism and scheduling
question: A varlen inference batch contains short prefills followed by a few very long-context decodes. Which FlashAttention-4 scheduling idea addresses the resulting slowdown?
options: Conditional softmax rescaling
Sorting batches by their per-tile cost so the longest work starts first (LPT)
Emulating the exponential on FMA units
Switching to FP8
explain: This is load imbalance: if long work is processed last, a few SMs finish late while others sit idle. The paper launches a small preprocessing kernel to sort batches by cost and write a virtual-to-actual batch index map, which can be cached so sorting costs nothing on later calls.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Load-balanced scheduling, plan and run, and CUDA graphs
question: An engine calls plan() before every layer's run() in a 32-layer model. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, plan must precede every run
plan() must be called only once at startup
run() will use the wrong KV pages
It repeats identical CPU scheduling 32 times per step, since all layers share the same lengths
explain: The plan depends only on the sequence lengths and page arrays, which are the same for every layer in a step. The docs and paper design plan for reuse across all layers; calling it per layer adds CPU overhead to every step. Calling it only at startup is also wrong, because lengths change every step.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Generating data by following a velocity field from noise
question: Why was maximum-likelihood training of continuous normalizing flows expensive compared with flow matching?
options: The loss required simulating the ODE (and backpropagating through it) on every training step
The network had to output a full probability density instead of a velocity
Maximum likelihood cannot be used with Gaussian noise
It needed a discriminator network as in a GAN
explain: Likelihood training of a CNF integrates the ODE inside the training loop. Flow matching regresses the network onto a closed-form target velocity at a sampled point, so no simulation happens during training.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Relation to diffusion, and rectified flow in Stable Diffusion 3
question: Which statement best describes the relation between diffusion models and flow matching?
options: They are unrelated; diffusion requires an SDE and cannot be sampled with an ODE
Diffusion paths are Gaussian conditional paths within the flow matching framework, and diffusion models can be sampled with the probability flow ODE
Flow matching is a special case of DDPM with a different noise schedule
Flow matching can only learn straight paths, diffusion can learn curved ones
explain: Lipman et al. recover VE and VP diffusion paths as Gaussian conditional paths, and Song et al.'s probability flow ODE gives diffusion models a deterministic sampler. The marginal flow of any of these, including OT paths, can be curved.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Inductive invariants: from bounded checks to every N
question: In the TLAPS proof, which assumption lets the same proof cover 3, 5 or 1,001 acceptors?
options: AllowRestart = FALSE
Any two quorums intersect
Values has exactly two elements
TypeOK
explain: Step <1>3 needs one acceptor in both quorums, and QuorumsMeet supplies it for any size. NoRestart is needed too, but it is about the environment, not the size. The proof never mentions how many acceptors or values exist.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Ghost permissions, VerusSync and what a proof trusts
question: A Verus project verifies cleanly, yet in production the service corrupts data. Which explanation is NOT possible if Verus and Z3 are sound?
options: The top-level ensures clause did not state the property that matters
The verified exec function returned a value violating its ensures clause on some input
A trusted spec of an external crate was wrong
The code contains assume(...) that is false
explain: If the tools are sound and nothing false is assumed, every verified function satisfies its ensures on every input. Failures come from what was assumed or trusted, or from specs that say the wrong thing.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Fine-grained FP8 at scale: tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion
question: An FP8 GEMM with K = 8192 shows growing error versus a BF16 reference, even though inputs are well scaled. What is the most likely cause and fix?
